terrain.difficultyNotes: The Skiway publishes a three-way split of 25% beginner, 50% intermediate and 25% expert. Its top tier is stored in percentAdvanced with percentExpert null, because this schema fills its grades in order and cannot record a third tier as a fourth - but note that the resort's own word for that 25% is expert, not advanced. OnTheSnow splits the same mountain four ways at 21/50/25/4, which is close enough to be reassuring. The base elevation is the one figure that needed adjudicating: the resort's mountain page states "the base elevation is 968 feet" and "the vertical drop is 968 feet" in the same sentence, which cannot both be true against a 1,943 ft summit. OnTheSnow's 974 ft base reconciles the summit and the vertical almost exactly, so the resort's 968 is treated as a duplication error and OnTheSnow's figure is stored for the base while the resort's 968 stands for the vertical. Two further things to know: the Skiway is two facing mountains rather than one, Holt's Ledge and Winslow, each with its own chairlift, and the Indy Pass partner listing carries badly wrong elevations for it - a 1,680 ft summit and a 700 ft base - which should not be used.

passes.name: Indy Pass
passes.access: Two all-day lift tickets per season on the Indy Pass. Skiway season passholders can also buy the discounted Indy AddOn Pass. The Skiway makes a point of the redemption being frictionless - its own wording is "No reservations needed for Indy!", which is a pointed contrast with the Indy partners that now require one.
passes.blackouts: None. The Indy partner page for the Skiway carries an explicit No Blackout Dates marker, and the resort confirms that Indy holders simply present the pass at the ticket window.

passes.name: Skiway partner-mountain discounts
passes.access: Not a pass but a benefit worth knowing: a Skiway season pass carries discounts at five other independent New England areas - Whaleback, Ragged, Saskadena Six, Middlebury Snowbowl and Pats Peak. Passholders also get two 50% off lift tickets for friends or family, and 10% off retail, rental and repair.
passes.blackouts: The resort states that blackout dates may apply to the partner-mountain discounts without publishing which dates or which mountains.

passes.name: Uphill New England
passes.access: A multi-mountain season pass for uphill travel only - skinning up rather than riding a lift - run by a non-profit and covering 24 New England mountains including this one. It buys no lift access at all. Worth recording because it is the only multi-mountain product on this roster aimed at a category of skier the lift-ticket economy ignores entirely.
passes.blackouts: No blackout dates are published; each mountain's own uphill policy and operating-hours restrictions apply.

pricing.notes: The cheapest lift-served skiing on this roster by a wide margin, and the pricing is refreshingly plain. Adult (18-64) weekday and non-peak: $35 online, $40 at the window. Peak, meaning weekends and some holidays: $60 online, $65 at the window. Twilight tickets, valid 1pm to 4pm, are $30 online and $35 at the window off-peak. The advanceTypical figure is the $35 non-peak online rate, which is the rate most visitors actually pay at a mountain whose busiest constituency is a college. Under-6s and over-80s ski free, on both day tickets and season passes, at all times including peak periods. The season pass figure is the 2025-26 general-public adult early-bird rate of $499, rising to $599 in season; no 2026-27 rates had been published on the verified date. The Dartmouth rates underneath it are the point of the place: $199 for an active full-time Dartmouth student, $59 for a first-year, $219 for a Dartmouth or DHMC employee at early-bird.

editorial.overview: The Dartmouth Skiway is two facing hills in Lyme Center owned by the Trustees of Dartmouth College, and it makes no attempt to be anything more than that. Its own about page opens by listing what you do not come here for - champagne powder, thousands of feet of vertical, high-speed quads, a gourmet lunch - which is the most honest piece of resort copy on this roster. What you get is 968 feet of vertical on 104 acres, 28 trails split evenly a quarter beginner, half intermediate and a quarter expert, two chairlifts and two carpets, a 1.25-mile run called Big Green, and an adult day ticket at $35 on a weekday. It opened in 1956 and it is the physical expression of a ski legacy that runs through Dartmouth's hundred-plus Olympian alumni and its ski team, and through the Ford Sayre youth programme that still trains here. The 17,000-square-foot McLane Family Lodge, finished in 2001 in white pine and New Hampshire granite, won an architecture award and is a genuinely lovely building to warm up in. Lifts run 9 to 4. There is no night skiing, the natural snowfall is 54 inches, and none of that is really the point.
editorial.snowQuality: Fifty-four inches a year is a thin natural total even for the Upper Valley, and the Skiway's answer is partial rather than total: snowmaking capacity covers over 60 of the 104 acres, so a bit under two thirds of the mountain. That is enough to hold the main trail network together through a normal winter and not enough to make the place bulletproof in a thaw. The elevation does not help - a 974-foot base and a 1,943-foot summit puts the whole mountain below the height at which New Hampshire winters get reliable - and the two-hill layout means the west-facing and east-facing sides hold snow differently through a sunny day. What the Skiway has instead is a Dartmouth-sized grooming operation on a small footprint, and the practical result is consistently decent corduroy on a mountain nobody is fighting you for.
editorial.crowds: Almost never a problem. Four lifts on 104 acres serving a college of 6,500 and an Upper Valley community that mostly skis Killington or Sunapee when it wants a day out means the Skiway operates at the density of a good local hill rather than a resort. The busy moments are structural rather than seasonal: Dartmouth ski team training on the competition trail, Ford Sayre youth sessions, and race weekends, all of which occupy specific terrain rather than filling the mountain. A free campus shuttle brings students out, which concentrates arrivals rather than spreading them. On a midweek afternoon in February you will have most of two mountains to yourself for $35.
editorial.difficulty: Even and modest. A quarter of the trails carry the resort's top rating - which the Skiway calls expert rather than advanced - half are intermediate, and a quarter beginner, on 968 feet of vertical. The two-mountain layout is what makes it more interesting than those numbers: Holt's Ledge and Winslow face each other across the base area, each served by its own chair, so a day here is two distinct mountains rather than laps on one. Big Green runs a mile and a quarter, which is a long way on this vertical and means the trails traverse rather than plunge. The competition trail is where the Dartmouth racers train and it holds real pitch. Nobody should come expecting to be tested for a full day, but the Skiway is a considerably better mountain to learn on and to carve on than a college hill has to be.

keyTrails.name: Big Green
keyTrails.note: The longest trail at 1.25 miles, and named for Dartmouth's colours. On 968 feet of vertical a run that length means gradient traded for time on the snow.

keyTrails.name: Holt's Ledge Double
keyTrails.note: The chair up the higher of the two hills, and the one that reaches the 1,943-foot summit. The natural ledge above it is the highest ground on the property.

keyTrails.name: Winslow Mountain Quad
keyTrails.note: The other half of the ski area, facing Holt's Ledge across the base. Having a quad on one side and a double on the other tells you where the traffic goes.

keyTrails.name: Big Bear and Little Cub carpets
keyTrails.note: The two learning carpets at the base by the McLane Family Lodge. A quarter of the Skiway's terrain is beginner and this is where all of it starts.

tidbits: The Skiway is owned by the Trustees of Dartmouth College and has run since 1956.
It is two facing mountains, Holt's Ledge and Winslow, each with its own chairlift.
An adult weekday lift ticket is $35 online - the cheapest on this roster.
An active full-time Dartmouth student pays $199 for a season pass; a first-year pays $59.
Under-6s and over-80s ski free, on both tickets and season passes, even at peak.
The 17,000-square-foot McLane Family Lodge won the 2002 New Hampshire AIA Excellence in Architecture Award.
A Skiway pass carries discounts at Whaleback, Ragged, Saskadena Six, Middlebury Snowbowl and Pats Peak.
Indy Pass holders need no reservation here, which is increasingly unusual.
The resort's own about page lists what you do not come here for before it lists what you do.
bestFor: The cheapest day on this roster

reviews.gist: Rates it well-financed and well-kept, a place to escape to on the days the big mountains are unbearable — a thousand feet of vertical over two faces of twisting New England trails, at a price that reflects who owns it. The qualifications are structural and he says they are not going away: the lifts are slow and will stay slow, neither side reaches its own summit because the Appalachian Trail crosses Holt’s Ledge, and the road between the two faces means walking. His interest is in whether a college-owned nonprofit can be a model for small mountains rather than in whether it competes with its neighbours.

moguls.bestTiming.note: Follows from moguls.quality - with no account of the ungroomed terrain there is nothing to time

moguls.bumpCulture.note: No mogul competitions or organised bump scene are documented. The Skiway's competitive tradition is alpine racing, through the Dartmouth ski team and the Ford Sayre programme

moguls.quality.note: No source describes the Skiway's bump skiing. The resort publishes a difficulty split but no trail list beyond Big Green and nothing about grooming policy, and PeakRankings has no Dartmouth Skiway page

parks.count.note: The Indy Pass partner directory's structured Terrain Parks field reads Yes, so the Skiway has at least one park. Nothing else is available: the resort's own site never mentions a terrain park on any page and names none, and OnTheSnow publishes no park count. Treat the Indy field with some caution here - the same listing carries elevations for the Skiway that are plainly wrong

parks.pipe.note: No pipe is mentioned by any source. With no park information from the resort there is nothing to read either way

size.snowmakingPercent.note: The resort states snowmaking capacity over 60 acres rather than a percentage. Sixty of 104 acres would be about 58%, but the resort's figure is an open-ended "over 60" and dividing it would put a false precision on the result

terrain.glades.note: Neither the resort, OnTheSnow nor the Indy partner listing mentions glades or tree skiing at the Skiway. Left null rather than assumed either way

terrain.percentExpert.note: The Skiway publishes three grades, not four, so there is no fourth-tier figure to source. Worth noting that the resort names its own top tier expert rather than advanced; this schema stores it in percentAdvanced because it fills grades in order

moguls.policy: No grooming policy is published, but the shape of the operation points one way. A college-owned ski area whose principal users are its own ski team, the Ford Sayre youth racing programme and a beginner-heavy public needs consistent, firm, groomed surfaces, and it has 104 acres and four lifts to maintain rather than a sprawling network. Snowmaking reaches over 60 of those acres, which is the part that must be groomed to survive. With 54 inches of natural snow a year there is rarely enough loose surface on the remaining terrain for bumps to build in the first place. Recorded as rare on that basis, and flagged for re-checking against the live grooming report in January.

parks.overview: The Indy Pass partner directory says the Skiway has terrain parks, and nothing else does. The resort's own site - which publishes its acreage, its difficulty split, its snowmaking capacity, its longest trail and its architecture award - never mentions a park anywhere, and neither does OnTheSnow. The Indy field carries less weight here than it does elsewhere on this roster, because the same listing gets the Skiway's summit and base elevations badly wrong. `nightPark` is false only because there is no night skiing at all.
